questions.q: A diatomic gas $(\gamma=1.4)$ does $100 \mathrm{~J}$ of work in an isobaric expansion. The heat given to the gas is :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
For Isobaric process $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{w}=\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}=100 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{u}+\mathrm{w} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{2} \mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}+\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{f}}{2}+1\right) \mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\ & \left(\frac{5}{2}+1\right) 100=350 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$
SECTION - B

questions.q:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : If $dQ$~and $dW$ represent the heat supplied to the system and the work done on the system respectively. Then according to the first law of thermodynamics $dQ = dU - dW$.

Reason R : First law of thermodynamics is based on law of conservation of energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below :
options: A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The first law of thermodynamics is stated as& $dQ = dU - dW$. Since~$dQ$~is heat supplied to~the system and positive thus,~$dW$& is work done on the system, i.e., negative& work.

We know that& the first law of thermodynamics deals with work done, and heat energy supplied or removed from a system. Therefore, it is based on the conservation of energy. The& law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another.

questions.q: A certain amount of gas of volume $V$ at $27 ° C$ temperature and pressure $2 \times {10}^{7}Nm^{- 2}$ expands isothermally until its volume gets doubled. Later it expands adiabatically until its volume gets redoubled. The final pressure of the gas will be (Use $\gamma = 1 . 5$)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given here,& ${P}_{1} = 2 \times {10}^{7}Nm^{- 2} = 2 \times {10}^{7}Pa$

Using Boyle's law,

${P}_{1}{V}_{1} = {P}_{2}{V}_{2}$

Since ${V}_{2} = 2{V}_{1}$.

Hence,~${P}_{2} = \dfrac{P1}{2}$~(isothermal expansion)

${P}_{2} = 1 \times {10}^{7}Pa$

Now, during adiabatic expansion,~

${P}_{2}\left({V}_{2}\right)\gamma = {P}_{3}\left(2{V}_{2}\right)\gamma$

${P}_{3} = \dfrac{1 \times {10}^{7}}{21 . 5} = 3 . 536 \times {10}^{6}Pa$

questions.q: A source supplies heat to a system at the rate of& $1000W .$ If the system performs work at a rate of $200W .$ The rate at which internal energy of the system increases is
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics,& $Q = W + U$.

Upon differentiation, we get~

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dW}{dt} + \dfrac{dU}{dt} ⇒ \dfrac{dU}{dt} = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} - \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Given:~$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 1000W$

$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 200W$

Therefore,~$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 1000W - 200W = 800W$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{0.4}{100}=\frac{1}{T} \\ & T=250 \mathrm{~K}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $n$ moles of an ideal gas with constant volume heat capacity ${C}_{v}$ undergo an isobaric expansion by certain volume. The ratio of the work done in the process, to the heat supplied is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
From First Law of thermodynamics,
$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Deltaw$
$\dfrac{\Deltaw}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \dfrac{\Delta U}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \dfrac{n{c}_{v}\Delta T}{n{c}_{p}\Delta T}$
$= 1 - \dfrac{{c}_{v}}{R + {c}_{v}}$
$= \dfrac{R}{R + {c}_{v}}$
As, $n{c}_{v} = {C}_{v}$
$\dfrac{\Deltaw}{\Delta Q} = \dfrac{nR}{{C}_{v} + nR}$

questions.q:
If one mole of an ideal gas at \left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}\right)$ is allowed to expand reversibly and isothermally ($A$ to $B$) its pressure is reduced to one-half of the original pressure (see figure). This is followed by a constant volume cooling till its pressure is reduced to one-fourth of the initial value \left(B \to C\right) .$~Then it is restored to its initial state by a reversible adiabatic compression ($C$ to $A). The net workdone by the gas is equal to:

$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$A - B =$ isothermal process

${W}_{AB} = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}\ln \left[\dfrac{2{V}_{1}}{{V}_{1}}\right] = {{P}_{1}{V}_{1}\ln \left($2\right)$

$B - C \to$ Isochoric process

${W}_{BC} = 0$

$C - A \to$Adiabatic process

${W}_{CA} = $\dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - \dfrac{P1}{4} \times 2{V}_{1}}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right]}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}

${W}_{net} = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + ${W}_{CA}\left\{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} = RT\right\}$

={P}_{1}{V}_{1}\ln \left($2\right) + 0 + $\dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}

${W}_{net} = RT \left[$\ln \left(2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]$

questions.q:
$7$ mole of certain monoatomic ideal gas undergoes a temperature increase of $40K$ at constant pressure. The increase in the internal energy of the gas in this process is
(Given $R = 8 . 3JK^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1}$)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
For the given process& pressure is constant therefore, it is an isobaric process.

For a quasi-static process the change in internal energy of an ideal gas is independent of the nature of the process and is given by,

$\Delta U = n{C}_{v}\Delta T$

$= n \times \dfrac{3R}{2} \times \Delta T$

[molar heat capacity at constant volume for monatomic gas $= \dfrac{3R}{2}$]

$\Delta U = 7 \times \dfrac{3}{2} \times 8 . 3 \times 40 = 3486J$

questions.q: In an adiabatic process, the density of a diatomic gas becomes $32n$~times its initial value. The final pressure of the gas is found to be~$n$ times the initial pressure. The value of $n$ is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given,

Final& density of diatomic gas is ${ρ}_{f} = 32n{ρ}_{i}$

Final pressure is~${P}_{f} = n{P}_{i}$

In adiabatic process, equation of state is given by,

$PV^{γ} = \text{constant} . . . \left(1\right)$

Where,~$V$~is the volume,~$P$~is the pressure and~$\gamma = $\dfrac{7}{5}~is the ratio of specific heat of diatomic gas

$P \left(\dfrac{m}{ρ}\right)\gamma = \text{constant} . . . \left(2\right)$, As~$V = \dfrac{m}{ρ}$

and mass is constant, then the~pressure is given by

$∴ P ∝ {ρ}^{γ}$

$⇒ \dfrac{Pf}{Pi} = \left(\dfrac{ρf}{ρi}\right)\gamma$

$⇒ \dfrac{n{P}_{i}}{Pi} = \left(\dfrac{32{ρ}_{i}}{ρi}\right){}^{7 / 5} = (32{)}^{7 / 5}$

$∴ n = {2}^{7} = 128$

questions.q:
The temperature of $3 . 00mol$~of an ideal diatomic gas is increased by $40 . 0 ° C$ without changing the pressure of the gas. The molecules in the gas rotate but do not oscillate. If the ratio of change in internal energy of the gas to the amount of workdone by the gas is $\dfrac{x}{10} .$~Then the value of $x$ (round off to the nearest integer) is~_________ .$

$($ Given \leftR = 8 . 31J{mol}^{- 1}K^{- 1})$

$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
First, recall the formula of change in internal energy in terms of molar specific heat at constant volume and change in temperature,& $∆ U = n{C}_{V}\Delta T$, for diatomic gas,~${C}_{V} = \dfrac{f}{2}R = \dfrac{5}{2}R$,~$⇒ ∆ U = n \times \dfrac{5}{2} \times R\Delta T$

$⇒ \dfrac{\Delta U}{W} = \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{2}nR\Delta T}{nR\Delta T} = \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{25}{10}$

So, $x = 25$

questions.q:
The pressure ${P}_{1}$~and density ${d}_{1}$ of diatomic gas \left(\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}\right)$ changes suddenly to ${P}_{2} \left(> {P}_{1}\right)$ and ${d}_{2}$ respectively during an adiabatic process. The temperature of the gas increases and becomes____times of its initial temperature.~

(given \dfrac{d2}{{d}_{1}} =$32$)

$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
For adiabatic process,& $PV^{γ} =$ constant

We know, density~$d = \dfrac{mass}{Volume}$.

Then, we have~$\dfrac{P}{d\gamma} =$ constant

Given here,~$\dfrac{d2}{{d}_{1}} = 32$~and~$\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}$.

The ratio~$\dfrac{P1}{P2} = \left(\dfrac{d1}{{d}_{2}}\right)\gamma = \left(\dfrac{1}{32}\right)\dfrac{7}{5} = \dfrac{1}{128}$

The ratio of temperature using ideal gas equation is~$\dfrac{T1}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{{P}_{2}{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{128} \times 32 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus,~${T}_{2} = 4{T}_{1}$.
